description: How solar PV went from lab curiosity to a global gigawatt titan — and how wind climbed while coal finally started to fall.
youtube_description:
The Solar Slingshot — 2006→2026 (with 2025–26 estimates)

Chapters:
0:00 Intro — why energy charts tell the century’s story
0:18 2006–2010 — solar is tiny, wind builds momentum
1:05 2011–2015 — subsidies, China scale, solar acceleration
2:00 2016–2019 — prices crash, installations explode
3:00 2020–2022 — record years, solar hits ~1,000 GW
3:55 2023–2026 — (est.) the slingshot: solar catches up to coal
4:30 Winners & losers: policy, supply chains, stranded assets
5:15 Sources & how we modeled 2025–26 estimates
5:45 Outro & call to action

Video summary:
This chart-race animation tracks cumulative global capacity in gigawatts (GW) for solar PV, wind (onshore+offshore), and coal-fired power from 2006 through 2026. Solar grows from ~5 GW in 2006 to ~1,450 GW by 2024 — and our projection shows roughly 2,000 GW by 2026. Wind rises steadily, hitting ~1,200 GW by 2024. Coal capacity climbs into the late 2010s, peaks around ~1,970 GW in 2021, and then edges down as retirements and moratoria accelerate.

Why it matters: the chart shows a literal energy slingshot — solar went from near-zero to a primary source within two decades, while coal’s dominance erodes. Expect regions with heavy renewables (EU, China, US) to force faster retirements of coal plants and change global electricity markets.

Sources: International Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA) capacity reports, IEA World Energy Outlook & electricity statistics, BloombergNEF (BNEF), Global Energy Monitor coal plant databases, national statistical offices. 2025–2026 values are modelled projections based on 2019–2024 installation trends, announced policies, and large-scale project pipelines.

If you want the raw CSV and source links, subscribe and check the pinned comment — I’ll publish the dataset and timestamps for download.

instagram_caption:
🚀 The solar revolution that outran coal — and nobody saw the slingshot coming.

Ten years ago solar PV was a niche: global cumulative capacity was roughly 5 GW in 2006. Fast-forward to 2016 and we’re at 303 GW. Fast-forward again to 2024 and solar had ballooned to ~1,450 GW — a 290x growth from 2006. That’s the scale shift that rewired electricity markets.

The story is a race. Wind accelerated too — from ~74 GW in 2006 to ~1,200 GW by 2024 — steady, powerful, predictable. Coal looked stable for years: global coal-fired capacity rose into the late 2010s and peaked near ~1,970 GW in 2021. But the turning point is clear: since 2021 retirements, moratoria, and finance pullback have pushed coal to ~1,920 GW in 2024 and a modeled decline toward ~1,830 GW by 2026.

Key milestones: cheap panels (module prices fell ~90% since 2010), China’s massive factory scale and installation programs after 2013, and record installation years in 2020–2022 pushed solar past the 1 TW milestone in 2022. That’s why our visualization shows solar rocketing while coal slowly deflates — the slingshot effect.

What surprised me most? The compounding effect: each year of gigawatts installed begets bigger manufacturing capacity and lower prices the next year. In the model we used, solar reaches ~2,000 GW by 2026 (projection), while coal drops below ~1,830 GW — a symbolic overtaking that marks a structural shift in where new electricity comes from.

What do you think will break first: coal’s final strongholds, or grid integration limits for ultra-high renewables? Tell me one country you think will flip completely to renew first — comment below. If you want more deep-dive charts like this, follow for weekly data animations.

The Solar Slingshot: how solar went from 5 GW in 2006 to ~1,450 GW by 2024 and is projected to hit ~2,000 GW by 2026. Wind climbed steadily to ~1,200 GW by 2024, while global coal-fired capacity — which peaked near ~1,970 GW in 2021 — has started to fall as retirements and financing restrictions mount.

This timeline comparison uses cumulative capacity (GW) to show how quickly utility-scale and distributed solar installations scaled after 2010, driven by module-price collapses, manufacturing scale (notably in China), and supportive policy. The result: a dramatic chart-race where solar’s line arcs upward and coal’s line, long flat, begins to slope down.

Sources include IRENA, IEA, BloombergNEF and Global Energy Monitor. 2025–2026 numbers in the visualization are projections based on announced projects and installation trends.
